title: ACB OFFLOAD
meta: SOP v5.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · Drill site to demob

steps.t: Get the North Slope Manifest from the mud engineer — review it, sign it, full asset numbers
steps.w: You left the rig with no manifest. DS 1B turns you around at the gate and the whole run is windshield time.

steps.t: Call DS 1B WIF — give them your departure and ETA
steps.w: Nobody at DS 1B knows you're coming. You'll sit on the pad while they figure out what to do with you.

steps.t: Talk the travel plan with your Lead — check weather and phase conditions with security
steps.w: Phase 3 closes the road while you're halfway there. Now you're parked in a whiteout with a loaded box.

steps.t: Pull onto the DS 1B pad — call the G&I operator and get approval before proceeding
steps.w: You rolled onto their pad uninvited. That phone call to MagTec isn't going to be about your driving skills.

steps.t: Stage at the staging area — tractor brakes set, duck ponds under the truck
steps.w: No ponds under the truck. One drip on the pad and you're filling out a spill report instead of driving.

steps.t: Check in with DS 1B personnel — hand over the completed manifest
steps.w: They can't take custody of what they can't verify. No manifest in hand, no offload.

steps.t: Walk down the HVAC and offload area — then complete and sign the fluid transfer permit
steps.w: No permit, no transfer. Open a valve before the paperwork and it's a stop-work, not a shortcut.

steps.t: Back in with the DS 1B spotter — driver-side rear chassis wheel to the MI Swaco chock
steps.w: You backed in blind. The spotter exists because the guy who didn't use one put a trailer through the containment.

steps.t: Set it up: brakes on, front wheel chocked, ponds down, PTO engaged, idle at 1,200
steps.w: Truck's not secured. It creeps six inches with hoses hooked and you're buying camlocks and explaining a spill.

steps.t: Connect the grounding and bonding strap to the tractor
steps.w: No bond, no ground. One static pop around vapors and you're the incident everyone trains on next year.

steps.t: Crack the 4" suction valve slow to bleed the vacuum — three points of contact on the deck
steps.w: That box is under vacuum. Yank a fitting first and it lets you know — hard, and right at face height.

steps.t: Clear the exclusion zones — both sides of the trailer and behind it
steps.w: There's a man standing where the box rolls. Everything stops now, or something much worse stops it later.

steps.t: Raise the rails 4"–6" at a time — roll the box back on tension, then drop the rails
steps.w: You jacked the rails full height in one shot. The box takes off, the cable snaps taut, and control is gone.

steps.t: Set both metal safety locks — one each side, working from the ground
steps.w: No locks in. The box shifts mid-offload, shears the fittings, and you're wearing what was inside.

steps.t: Connect the 4" manifold hose to the ACB suction — pond under the fitting, gaskets checked, Velcro on
steps.w: Bad gasket, no pond. It weeps mud the whole offload and you find out when the operator does.

steps.t: Connect the DS 1B 6" pump hose to the discharge — pond first, gaskets checked, Velcro on
steps.w: Free liquid under that cap. Pull it with no pond down and the pad gets a sample.

steps.t: Line up the manifold — Valve A open, Valve B open, Valve C closed
steps.w: Wrong lineup. You just sent flow somewhere it was never supposed to go, and the scrubber knows it.

steps.t: Walk down every hose — camlocks tight, Velcro wrapped, ponds under all connections
steps.w: The connection you didn't check is the one that lets go under flow. It always is.

steps.t: Start the HVAC — spotter has eyes on you, then tilt the rails 1 to 2 feet
steps.w: You tilted a loaded box with no spotter and no suction running. Nobody watching, nothing catching.

steps.t: On the operator's call — open the 6" discharge and stand where he puts you
steps.w: He didn't call it. You opened his facility's line on your own clock — that's his job you just did wrong.

steps.t: Box empty, on the call — close the 6", shut Valve B, open Valve C for suction
steps.w: Skip the suction lineup and the residual sits in the line, frozen solid by the time someone finds it.

steps.t: Clear the line on the call — open the 6", then close it when he calls it
steps.w: That clear-out runs on his direction, both ways. Guessing at it leaves mud in his line with your name on it.

steps.t: Shut down the HVAC by procedure — no E-stop — open Valve B, check the scrubber tank
steps.w: You hit the E-stop like an off switch. Now it's a reset, a breaker check, and a story you tell the mechanic.

steps.t: Break it down in order — 6" off, 4" off and stowed, plugs in, ground strap back in its spot
steps.w: Hoses off before shutdown and lineup? Whatever's still in them goes on your boots and the pad.

steps.t: Pull the safety locks — stow them on the tractor deck behind the cab
steps.w: Winch against set locks and something gives. It won't be the locks.

steps.t: Winch the box up until it seats in the locking hooks — then eyes on the pins, engaged behind the rollers
steps.w: Pins not verified. That box rides forty miles of haul road held on by hope.

steps.t: 360 walkaround — hoses clear, people clear, then grab your ponds and stow them in the HVAC
steps.w: Roll out without the 360 and the 6" hose you're still hooked to comes along for the ride.

steps.t: PTO off, brakes off — head back to the rig
steps.w: Driving with the PTO engaged. The pump runs dry all the way home and dies quiet, halfway through the next job.

title: ACB LOADING AT RIG
meta: SOP v2.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · Walkdown to shutdown

steps.t: Walk down every hose on the ACB, cuttings box, and HVAC — camlocks gasketed and locked, Velcro or pins on, ponds under every fitting
steps.w: The fitting you didn't walk lets go under vacuum. Now you're chasing mud instead of loading it.

steps.t: Mechanical room check — shore power cable plugged at the door, toggle set to match: shore power or Gen
steps.w: Toggle's on Gen with shore power plugged. Best case nothing runs. Worst case you cook something expensive.

steps.t: Front panel: verify the level gauge sweeps Empty to Full — if it won't rotate, stop and get the Foreman
steps.w: Gauge is stuck and you loaded anyway. First warning you get that the box is full is the scrubber eating mud.

steps.t: Set the valves: 4" suction OPEN and strapped, 6" discharge CLOSED and capped, 4" fill CLOSED and locked
steps.w: One valve in the wrong position and the flow path goes somewhere you didn't plan. The mud doesn't care which valve it was.

steps.t: Check the dump door seal and torque the roof hatch wing nuts — vacuum holds on the ACB
steps.w: Bad seal, loose hatch. The box can't pull vacuum and every fitting weeps all shift.

steps.t: Open the scrubber drain valve — verify it's empty, then close and tighten it
steps.w: Fluid was already sitting in the scrubber and you started anyway. Now it's in the blower.

steps.t: Verify the blue relief valve is OPEN — wheel all the way left, vac switch open
steps.w: You started against a closed relief. That system builds pressure with nowhere to send it — that's how gaskets and eardrums go.

steps.t: Check blower oil in the sight glasses — between 1/8 and 1/2 full — and E-stop pulled out
steps.w: Dry blower, engaged E-stop, or both. Either way you just tried to start a machine that was telling you no.

steps.t: Master power ON, then hit START below the LED display
steps.w: You're flipping switches out of order on a panel that has an order. That's how you stand there wondering why nothing runs.

steps.t: Vacuum toggle ON — hear it wind up — then close the relief valve, wheel to the right
steps.w: Relief closed before the vacuum's even running. You choked the system in the crib.

steps.t: With suction pulling: check the rear door and hatch wing nuts sealed — snug, not gorilla-tight — hydraulic locks down
steps.w: Over-torqued wing nuts crush the door seal. Now the box won't hold vacuum, and that seal costs more than your patience.

steps.t: Open the fill valve at the rear of the ACB — a hiss at the hose connection means recheck the gasket
steps.w: That hiss was the gasket telling you. Loading through a bad seal sprays mist all shift.

steps.t: Drop the stinger into the cuttings box once there's enough mud and cuttings to load
steps.w: Stinger down in an empty box just pulls air and burns the run. Wait for the mud.

steps.t: Watch the level gauge as it loads — the float can bury in cuttings, so verify it still moves free
steps.w: The float buried and you trusted it. The box overfilled quiet, and the scrubber took the rest.

steps.t: At full level: pull the stinger and clear the suction line to the box
steps.w: You shut down with a charged line. Everything in it is now everywhere it shouldn't be.

steps.t: Shut the fill valve FIRST to build suction in the box — then shut the suction line
steps.w: Backwards. Close suction first and there's no vacuum holding the box — the fill line drains where it stands.

steps.t: Confirm lines are clear and the ACB suction valve is closed
steps.w: Shut the machine down with product in the lines. It'll be frozen in there by morning.

steps.t: Vacuum toggle OFF to relieve — if it won't open the relief, open the blue valve by hand
steps.w: Vacuum never relieved. Whatever you do next happens to a system still under suction.

steps.t: VERIFY the relief is open — then and only then hit the red OFF for the motor
steps.w: You killed the motor under vacuum. The SOP prints that warning in bold because this exact move wrecks the unit.

steps.t: Open the scrubber drain into the pan — no moisture at all means check the drain isn't plugged
steps.w: Nothing drained and you called it clean. A plugged drain reads exactly the same as an empty scrubber — until it doesn't.

steps.t: Unhook suction and fill lines, check the gaskets, cap both ends of the ACB
steps.w: Open fittings on a loaded box headed for the road. Every bump is a chance to share the contents.

title: LOADING ON CHASSIS
meta: SOP v3.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · Spot-in to haul-out

steps.t: Park in the staging area, set the brakes — then eyes on the loading area: obstructions, people, chock placement, lighting
steps.w: You backed into an area you never looked at. Whatever was in it is now part of the job.

steps.t: Notify everyone in the area and set the exclusion zone
steps.w: Someone wandered in mid-move because nobody told them a move was happening. That's on the operator, not the walker.

steps.t: Talk it through with your spotter — intentions and hand signals, before the truck moves
steps.w: You and the spotter are running two different playbooks. His 'stop' looked like your 'keep coming.'

steps.t: Back in on the spotter's signals — lose sight of him, you stop. Tires to the chocks or his stop call
steps.w: You kept rolling after you lost him in the mirror. The rule is simple: no spotter in sight, no wheels turning.

steps.t: Lock it down: brakes set, ponds down, driver-side front wheel chocked, PTO on, idle 1,200
steps.w: Truck's live and loose. Everything you hook to it from here inherits that problem.

steps.t: Connect the grounding and bonding strap to the tractor chassis
steps.w: No bond. Static and product vapors settle their differences without you — once.

steps.t: Pull the plug and open the 4" suction butterfly SLOW — three points of contact on the deck
steps.w: Fast-cracked a valve on a box under vacuum, one hand on the truck. Pick which mistake bites first.

steps.t: Clear the exclusion zones — passenger side, driver side, behind the trailer
steps.w: A man in the roll path when the box moves. There is no version of that story that ends fine.

steps.t: Raise the rails 4–6 inches at a time on the spotter's eyes — keep cable tension, lower once the box is positioned
steps.w: Full lift, slack cable, no spotter. The box picked its own landing spot.

steps.t: Install both metal safety locks, left and right — then PTO off
steps.w: No locks and the hydraulics are still live. The box is held up by fluid pressure and optimism.

steps.t: Connect the 4" product line at the rear — containment under the valve before the cap comes off, three points of contact on the landing
steps.w: Cap off, no containment, one hand for the ladder. The free liquid in that cap area found the ground and you nearly did too.

steps.t: Walk the connections — gaskets, Velcro, ponds — then open the 4" ball valve and fill per SOP
steps.w: Valve open on unchecked connections. The weakest fitting just volunteered.

steps.t: Box full: clear the product line, shut the rear 4" ball valve
steps.w: Rolled with a charged line. It emptied itself across the pad on your way out.

steps.t: Close the 4" suction butterfly — no stem extension means a ladder and three points of contact
steps.w: Free-climbed the box to reach a valve. The fall protection rules weren't written for someone else.

steps.t: Shut down the HVAC per its SOP — E-stop is for emergencies only
steps.w: E-stop as a convenience button. Now there's a reset procedure, a breaker check, and a conversation.

steps.t: Disconnect the hoses — caps and plugs in, hose ends in containment, camlock ears secured on the ACB
steps.w: Open hose ends on the trailer deck. Forty miles of washboard road will find what's left in them.

steps.t: PTO back on — parking brake still set, wheels still chocked — pull the safety locks and stow them behind the cab
steps.w: Locks pulled with the truck unsecured. You removed the backup while the primary was already gambling.

steps.t: Engage the cable lever system — winch the box up until it seats in the locking hooks
steps.w: Box riding loose on the rails. First hard brake, it comes forward to meet you.

steps.t: Eyes on the locking pins — engaged behind the ACB rollers. Pins restrain the energy
steps.w: Nobody verified the pins. That's a loaded box held on by assumption at highway speed.

steps.t: 360 walkaround — people and obstacles clear — then pick up every duck pond and stow them
steps.w: Left the ponds on the pad and something under the truck in your blind spot. The 360 exists because mirrors lie.

title: CHASSIS GREASING
meta: SOP v2.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · #1 arctic synthetic, front to rear

steps.t: Set the parking brakes — truck AND trailer
steps.w: One brake set out of two. The half you skipped is the half that rolls while you're under it.

steps.t: Chock the truck and trailer tires
steps.w: No chocks. You're about to put your hands in pinch points on equipment that's free to move.

steps.t: Gather the kit — #1 arctic-grade synthetic, grease gun, rags — and get your PPE on
steps.w: Wrong grease for the Slope. Summer grease at forty below sets up like taffy and lubricates nothing.

steps.t: Raise the chassis trailer and set the safety stops
steps.w: Working under raised rails with no stops. Hydraulics hold until the moment they don't — that's the whole reason stops exist.

steps.t: Front cable sheaves and front cable ram pins — grease till you see flow and extrusion, wipe the excess
steps.w: Out of order and you'll lose track of what's done. Dry sheaves under load eat cables — front to rear, every time.

steps.t: Sheave block — grease until lubricant appears, wipe it down
steps.w: Skipped the sheave block. It runs dry under the cable load until the day it seizes mid-lift.

steps.t: Side rollers — rotate each roller WHILE greasing until it shows at the opposite side
steps.w: Greased a parked roller. The fresh grease sat on one spot and the bearing surface stayed dry — rotation is the whole trick.

steps.t: Lifting ram pins, upper and lower — grease until backflow shows
steps.w: No backflow means it never filled. Half-greased ram pins wear oval, and oval pins drop boxes.

steps.t: Landing gear points — 4 pumps per fitting
steps.w: Dry landing gear. It'll crank fine right up until it won't, on the coldest day, with a loaded box on it.

steps.t: Middle cable ram pins and center cable roller — grease with flow visible, rotate the roller
steps.w: The middle points are the ones everyone skips because they're awkward to reach. That's exactly why they fail first.

steps.t: Cable ram sheaves and rear pivot point — 5 to 6 shots each
steps.w: Rear pivot ran dry. Every lift works that joint, and a seized pivot turns a routine lift into a bent chassis.

steps.t: Tail roll while turning it, DOT bumper points 5–7 shots, S-cams one per wheel, slack adjusters 5–6 shots on both fittings
steps.w: Skipped the brake hardware. Dry S-cams and slack adjusters mean brakes that drag or don't — you find out on the ice.

steps.t: Continuous ops: full chassis grease every week
steps.w: Stretched the interval. Arctic loads on dry pins do a week of wear in a day.

steps.t: Inspect rollers, washers, cotter pins, and sheaves on the daily/weekly walkarounds
steps.w: The cotter pin you didn't look at backed out. The washer left, the roller followed.

steps.t: Rotate the side rollers every 3 months
steps.w: Rollers wearing one groove in one spot for a year. Rotation is free — replacement isn't.

steps.t: Caliper the brass bushings — replace the roller at 2.356" ID. Grooved side in, flat side out, washer, then a 5"×3/8" cotter pin bent tight
steps.w: Roller went back together backwards. Grooved side out means it chews the washer and walks off the pin.

title: TANK FARM OPS
meta: SOP v2.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · Walk-down to reporting

steps.t: Inspect the tank farm — spill signs inside and outside containment, containment integrity, snow and water buildup eating capacity
steps.w: Containment half-full of snowmelt. The capacity you're counting on in a spill isn't there.

steps.t: Check heaters, light plants, lighting, and that nothing is blocking vac truck access to the onload/offload areas
steps.w: Vac truck can't reach the connection point. Now there's improvising, and improvising around fluid transfer is how spills start.

steps.t: Walk the hoses and fittings — damage, caps and plugs installed, safety ties over the camlocks, tank ventilation clear
steps.w: Uncapped fitting, no safety tie. One bump and the camlock walks open with fluid behind it.

steps.t: Verify the safety gear — spill kit stocked, fall protection inspected and certified, ground straps in place
steps.w: The spill kit was empty when the spill happened. Checking it after is just inventory for the report.

steps.t: Documentation in order — SDS for the fluids on hand, fluid transfer sheets complete
steps.w: Nobody can say what's in the tank. Medics and responders need the SDS before the incident, not during.

steps.t: Team briefing — procedures, hazards, PPE, and everyone can trace the flow paths, tank volumes, and valve placement
steps.w: A hand on the transfer who can't trace the flow path. He'll open the valve he's standing next to, not the one that's right.

steps.t: Confirm the correct fluid is being transferred
steps.w: Wrong fluid in the wrong tank. That's not a transfer anymore, it's contamination with paperwork.

steps.t: Make sure the bleeder valve is in line
steps.w: No bleeder in the line. Trapped pressure has to go somewhere, and it picks the moment you break a connection.

steps.t: Use vacuum to verify the lines are clear before flow
steps.w: Pushed product into a line that still had product. The slug came out the far end where nobody expected it.

steps.t: Establish solid comms with the offloader or onloader — vac truck, rig, whoever's on the other end
steps.w: Two ends of one hose, no comms. One end opened, the other wasn't ready — the hose decided the rest.

steps.t: Trace and confirm the flow path to or from the tanks
steps.w: Flow went where the valves sent it, not where you meant it. Tanks don't take corrections.

steps.t: Open every valve needed for the transfer — then start it
steps.w: Started the pump against a closed valve. Pressure built until something opened on its own terms.

steps.t: Monitor tank levels the whole transfer — overfill is a spill you watched happen
steps.w: Walked away from a running transfer. The tank topped out with nobody watching the gauge.

steps.t: Transfer done — vacuum every line clear
steps.w: Product left standing in the lines, frozen by morning. Next crew inherits a plugged system and your name.

steps.t: Report to the Mud Engineer — fluids transferred and tank volumes. A spill goes up the chain NOW: MagTec Manager, Mud Engineer, ConocoPhillips Security, SLP HSE
steps.w: Unreported volumes, and if there was a drip, an unreported spill. On this pad that's not an oops — that's a career decision.

title: MONEY PIT OFFLOAD
meta: SOP v2.0 · Rev. 11/18/2025 · Approved D. Redick · Plan C only, Conoco authorization required

steps.t: Get approval from the ConocoPhillips infrastructure rep BEFORE proceeding to the Money Pit
steps.w: Money Pit is Plan C on Conoco's ground. Rolling in without their say-so turns a backup plan into an access violation.

steps.t: Use the ramp signed "ACB's Only" and pull up to the staging area
steps.w: Wrong ramp. Those signs sort traffic that doesn't mix — and the pit doesn't forgive improvisation.

steps.t: Disconnect the gate cable and secure it
steps.w: You worked around a barricade instead of opening it. The cable's there to control the ramp — leave it flapping and it controls nothing.

steps.t: Walk up and retract the bird netting — push pole to get it clear of the ACB lift path
steps.w: Netting still in the lift path. The box comes up, hooks the net, and now you're doing rigging repairs over a pit.

steps.t: Line up and back to the ramp stop — spotter if one's available
steps.w: Backed up a ramp over a pit by feel. The ramp stop is the last thing between your drive axle and the edge.

steps.t: Wheel chocks under the tires
steps.w: No chocks, nose-up on a ramp, about to shake a loaded box. The truck gets a vote on where it sits.

steps.t: PTO on — idle the tractor up
steps.w: No PTO, no hydraulics. Everything after this step is you pulling levers connected to nothing.

steps.t: Lift the ACB and shake it back to offload position
steps.w: Box never repositioned. Dump it from travel position and the load goes where gravity likes, not where the pit is.

steps.t: Lay it down, insert the safety latch, pull the rear 6" cap
steps.w: Cap off with no latch in. If the box shifts while you're behind it, you're in the worst spot on the Slope.

steps.t: Pick up to offload angle and open the back valve
steps.w: Valve open at the wrong angle. The flow's got its own opinion about trajectory now.

steps.t: Product out: lay it down, open the wing nuts and dogs, open the back hatch
steps.w: Wrestling the hatch hardware with the box still at angle. Every one of those dogs is a pinch point over your head.

steps.t: Safety latch on the rear door
steps.w: Unsecured door on a box you're about to tilt again. That door swings with real weight behind it.

steps.t: Lift back to dumping angle until every cutting is out
steps.w: Called it done half-full. The leftover freezes into ballast and rides back to the rig with you.

steps.t: Lay the chassis down
steps.w: Working the back of a raised box. Everything from here happens on the ground or it doesn't happen safe.

steps.t: Clean the rear seal and knock the cuttings off the back of the ACB and chassis
steps.w: Dirty seal, door closed on it. It leaks the whole ride home and the haul road gets a stripe.

steps.t: Remove the latch and secure the back door
steps.w: Latch left in or door left loose — either way that box isn't road-ready and won't announce it until it matters.

steps.t: Return the ACB to travel position
steps.w: Rolled out with the box at angle. First good bump resets your center of gravity for you.

steps.t: Pull off the ramp and put the bird netting back
steps.w: Netting left open over the pit. The reason it exists shows up on wings about ten minutes after you leave.

steps.t: Cable barricade back across the entrance
steps.w: Ramp left open behind you. The next truck in wasn't authorized, wasn't briefed, and now that's partly on you.

title: PISTEN BULLY
meta: SOP Rev. 2 · Approved D. Redick · Authorization to emergency response

steps.t: PB600 tutorial complete, check ride passed, formal sign-off from the Lead Operator — before any independent operation
steps.w: Nobody signed you off. An unauthorized operator in a machine this size isn't initiative, it's the first line of the incident report.

steps.t: Gear up: safety glasses, hi-vis outer, steel toes, hearing protection as required, real cold-weather gear
steps.w: Underdressed for the machine or the weather. The Slope doesn't grade on effort.

steps.t: Daily safety meeting done — and a JSA before any fabrication work
steps.w: Skipped the morning meeting. The hazard everyone else heard about this morning is the one you're about to find.

steps.t: Walkaround before initial movement — leaks, damage, mechanical issues. Deficiencies get fixed BEFORE you roll
steps.w: The leak you didn't walk past this morning is the trail of hydraulic fluid you're following back tonight.

steps.t: Three points of contact climbing in
steps.w: Jumped up like it's a pickup. Iced steps on a machine this tall turn a shortcut into a shoulder surgery.

steps.t: Seat belt on — all times, no exceptions
steps.w: No belt in a machine that can pitch sideways in terrain you can't always read. The cab only protects what stays inside it.

steps.t: Daily comms out: weather, trail conditions, wildlife, disabled vehicles, hazards
steps.w: Nobody knows your conditions or your route. When you go quiet out there, quiet is all they have to search with.

steps.t: Avoid backing — if you must, use a spotter. Shop entry and exit take a full walkaround plus a spotter
steps.w: Backed blind. A Pisten Bully doesn't feel what it rolls over, and neither will you until you get out.

steps.t: After every stop: walk it around again before moving
steps.w: Something changed while you were parked — a leak started, a track picked something up. The machine won't mention it.

phases.name: PARK IT & WHEN IT GOES WRONG

steps.t: Before you exit: blade DOWN, emergency brake SET, three points out — and mind the wind direction
steps.w: Blade up, no brake, and you're standing next to it. A parked machine that can still move isn't parked.

steps.t: Spill: stop the source if it's safe to reach — then absorbents down
steps.w: Watched it run while thinking about it. Every second of flow is more tundra in the report.

steps.t: Contaminated snow into approved bags — double-bagged, labeled, location documented
steps.w: Loose contaminated snow, no label, no location. Now it's not a cleanup, it's an unreported release.

steps.t: Notify your supervisor and the SLP Alaska HSE Rep
steps.w: Handled it quietly. An unreported spill on the Slope isn't discretion — it's the version of the story where you chose the consequences.

steps.t: Injury: evaluate on scene with the onboard kit — escalate to medevac via Starlink, sat phone, InReach SOS, or PLB
steps.w: Hesitated on the escalation call. Out there, the gap between 'probably fine' and medevac is measured in daylight and body heat.

title: CUTTING, GRINDING & HOT WORK
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Verify the hot work permit before a torch, saw or wheel comes out
steps.w: No permit means nobody checked the area. You light off in a spot no one cleared, and the fire, injury and equipment damage this SOP exists to stop all land at once.

steps.t: Pull every combustible out of the work area before you start
steps.w: Slag travels. It finds the one thing you left behind and lights it while your back is turned. That is the fire this whole document exists to prevent.

steps.t: Establish the fire watch and have them on station before the first cut
steps.w: Your eyes are on the cut and your face shield is down. A spark sets in behind you and you will not see it - the fire watch is the only person who will.

steps.t: Barricade the area so nobody walks into the work
steps.w: A hand cuts through your spark stream with nothing on and wears the slag. That is the injury the barricade was there to stop.

steps.t: Dress out - face shield, safety glasses, gloves, FR clothing, hearing protection, respirator if the job calls for it
steps.w: Sparks and slag land on you, not just the floor. Every item on that list is required because this work burns people - dress short and you take the injury this SOP is written to prevent.

steps.t: Run the torch, saw or grinder only within the manufacturer's limits for that equipment
steps.w: Those limits are the line this SOP draws around the tool. Work a machine past what the manufacturer rated it for and you are outside every control on this page - that is how the equipment damage and the injury happen.

steps.t: Contain your sparks and slag with fire blankets, shields and whatever else the job needs
steps.w: Loose slag does not stay where you are looking. It rolls under equipment and into corners and starts the fire behind you.

steps.t: Keep the fire watch on station the full 30 minutes after the last cut
steps.w: Hot metal holds heat long after you rack the torch. Cut the watch short and the fire starts after everyone has walked away, with nobody there to catch it.

title: DECALS AND LETTERING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Don't take the job until you're trained on surface prep and application technique
steps.w: Untrained, you're guessing at both. You guess at prep and you guess at technique, and what you get is the bubbling and peeling this SOP exists to prevent. Training in those two things is the price of doing this work at all.

steps.t: Safety glasses on, gloves on, proper footwear - before you start
steps.w: This SOP has one emergency and it's exposure or injury. When that happens the job stops and supervision gets the call. Glasses, gloves and the right footwear are what this document puts between you and that call.

steps.t: Pull the drawings, check the label spec, and look over the surface you're sticking to
steps.w: Three things to verify and skipping any one costs you. Skip the surface and you lay a decal on something that won't hold it - it bubbles, it lifts. Skip the print and the label you stuck down clean may be the wrong label.

steps.t: Clean the surface before the decal ever touches it
steps.w: Dirt under the adhesive. That's your bubbles and that's your peeling - the exact failure this procedure names and the reason cleaning comes first.

steps.t: Line it up accurate to the placement on the print - don't eyeball it
steps.w: Off-position and the adhesive has already grabbed. Correct placement is the installer's responsibility in this SOP - yours - and it gets checked again before that piece is released.

steps.t: Lay it down with the approved method - no trapped air, no lifted edges
steps.w: Wrong technique traps air under the decal. The SOP calls out bubbles and peeling by name, and the approved method is the only thing it gives you to keep them off your work.

steps.t: Inspect placement and adhesion before that piece gets released
steps.w: Release is the last checkpoint in this procedure. A label that's off-position or already lifting and clears you here isn't caught by anything else in this document - the inspection before release is the whole safety net.

title: EQUIPMENT TAGGING
sub: ASSET MARKING AND TRACEABILITY - KENAI FAB SHOP
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Be trained on asset identification and recordkeeping before you pick up a tag
steps.w: Untrained hand guessing at the format marks the wrong thing the wrong way, and it stays wrong until somebody downstream trips over it and has to stop the job.

steps.t: Wear safety glasses and gloves as required for the marking job
steps.w: This SOP calls for glasses and gloves and does not spell out what for. That is not your call to make at the bench - put them on, and if you do not know what this job puts in front of your eyes and hands, ask your supervisor before you start marking.

steps.t: Verify the asset numbers, tag formats, and documentation requirements before anything goes on the equipment
steps.w: Skip the check and you mark an asset with a number that belongs to something else. Work stops dead the day it's found.

steps.t: Apply the tags and markings to specification - no field improvising on format
steps.w: Mark it off-spec and it isn't the ID the asset system expects. The trail on that piece of iron breaks right there.

steps.t: Enter the information into the asset system accurately, right off the tag
steps.w: A digit off in the system and the record points at the wrong piece of iron for the rest of its life.

steps.t: Keep the records current so the asset can be traced through its whole life
steps.w: Records go cold and nobody can prove where that asset has been or what's been done to it.

steps.t: Find identification that doesn't match - stop the work and tell your supervisor
steps.w: Push on past a bad ID and the wrong asset goes back into service under somebody else's number.

title: SHOP HOUSEKEEPING
sub: KENAI FAB SHOP AND TOOL ROOM
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Get trained on housekeeping expectations and waste handling before you work an area
steps.w: Untrained hands guess at the waste stream and walk past the scrap. You inherit a shop full of the debris nobody knew was theirs to move.

steps.t: Safety glasses, gloves and proper footwear on before you touch a broom or a scrap bin
steps.w: Bare eyes and street shoes in a shop full of offcuts. The debris you are picking up finds your eyes, your palms and the top of your foot.

steps.t: Clear debris, spills and scrap out of your assigned area every day - do not let it build up
steps.w: Spills and scrap sit where they fell. Somebody's boot finds the slick spot or the offcut and they go down onto shop floor and steel.

steps.t: Keep walkways and exits clear - nothing stacked or staged in them
steps.w: Clear is the whole point of an exit. Stage material in one and the fast way out of the shop is a route nobody can use the one time it matters.

steps.t: Take every tool back to the tool room when you are done with it
steps.w: A tool that never comes back is a tool that gets damaged or goes missing - and until it does, it is one more thing on the floor of an area you are supposed to be keeping clear.

steps.t: Put each tool back in its designated location, not just inside the tool room door
steps.w: Tools dumped in the wrong spot get damaged or go missing, and the next hand runs the job with whatever is left.

steps.t: Put waste materials in the stream the site requires
steps.w: Waste that does not go out the way the site requires does not go out at all. It piles back up in the area you are supposed to clear every day, and the floor you cleaned this morning is a debris field again.

steps.t: Stop work on an unsafe condition and tell supervision - do not work around it
steps.w: Nobody stops, nobody gets told, and the condition stays exactly where it is until it catches the next hand who walks through.

title: LIFTING AND RIGGING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Keep untrained hands off the rigging - trained personnel run the lift
steps.w: Somebody guessing at the rigging is how a load ends up on the deck instead of the rack, and the man under it never picked the gear.

steps.t: Hard hat, gloves, safety glasses, steel toes, and hi-vis before you touch anything
steps.w: No hi-vis and you are not seen standing in the path of travel. No hard hat and the first thing that comes off that load lands where your skull is.

steps.t: Work out the load weight, center of gravity, rigging method, and path of travel
steps.w: Guess the weight and you are over the rating before it clears the floor. Guess the center of gravity and it shifts out of the rigging on the way up. Guess the path and you route it over somebody.

steps.t: Take the lift plan to the supervisor and get it approved before you rig
steps.w: Approval is the only check on your numbers. Skip it and the weight, the center of gravity and the path of travel are one man's arithmetic - and you find out which one was wrong after the load is already off the ground.

steps.t: Inspect the rigging before you use it
steps.w: Damaged rigging gives you no warning. It holds right up until the load is overhead, then lets go all at once.

steps.t: Settle the signals before the pick - standard hand signals, or radios where required
steps.w: The operator only knows what you tell him. Use something that is not a standard signal and your stop reads as keep coming - the load keeps traveling down the path you are standing in.

steps.t: Run tag lines on the load and keep communication clear the whole move
steps.w: A tag line is how you steer a load without a hand on it. Skip it and you are guiding by hand - so you are inside the load instead of clear of it when it goes.

steps.t: Stay inside rated capacity - the load, the rigging, all of it
steps.w: Over the rating is over the rating. The rigging fails at the worst moment, load overhead, and it comes down on the path of travel somebody is walking.

steps.t: Drop, near miss, or injury - stop the work and call supervision
steps.w: Work through it and the same rigging sets up the same drop an hour later, with nobody warned and nobody watching for it.

title: LOAD SECUREMENT
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Don't touch a binder until you're trained on securement regs and methods
steps.w: Untrained, you're guessing - which chain, which binder, how many. This SOP makes training the gate, because the load that teaches you is the one that shifts on you while you're rolling.

steps.t: Gloves, safety glasses and hi-vis on before you get on the deck
steps.w: Bare hands on chain and binders. Nothing over your eyes when gear under tension lets go. Nothing on you that makes you easy to pick out while you're working the trailer. The SOP names all three - wear all three.

steps.t: Walk the pre-transport inspection - weight distribution, securement devices, trailer condition
steps.w: Nobody looked. A bad weight split and a worn securement device go out together, and the road finds them both while you're in transit with no way to fix it.

steps.t: Secure the load with rated chains, binders and straps - rated gear only
steps.w: Unrated rope or whatever tie-down was in the box holds right up until it doesn't. Then you've got a shifting load and failed gear at once - the exact emergency this SOP tells you to stop the truck for.

steps.t: Driver and loader both confirm the load is secured per regulations before it moves
steps.w: It moves on nobody's say-so. The SOP puts it on both of you, driver and loader, and it puts it before transport - because that's the last point where fixing it costs you nothing but time.

steps.t: Recheck securement during transport - not just before you pulled out
steps.w: Securement you set tight doesn't stay the way you left it. The SOP requires a recheck once you're underway, because a load that has started to move gives you warning before it gives you an emergency.

steps.t: Load shifting or gear failing - stop the transport and call supervision
steps.w: Keep driving on a shifting load or failing gear and it gets worse with every mile you add to it, and nobody up the chain knows you're out there with it. Stop first, then notify - that's the order the SOP gives.

title: MECHANICAL ASSEMBLY
sub: ACBS, HVAC UNITS AND PUMP & FILTER SKIDS
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Don't touch the job unless you're trained on mechanical assembly, torqueing, and the hazards of that specific unit
steps.w: Untrained hand on an unfamiliar skid finds the pinch points the hard way - with a finger in one.

steps.t: Safety glasses, gloves and steel-toe boots on, plus whatever else the task calls for
steps.w: A component gets away from you and lands on a boot that isn't rated to take it. That's a crushed foot from exactly the dropped component this SOP makes you stop work for.

steps.t: Go through the drawings, BOMs, torque specs, lifting plan and pinch points before a tool comes out of the box
steps.w: Skip the review and you're guessing at torque, guessing at the lift, and meeting a pinch point nobody warned you about.

phases.name: BUILD IT AND SIGN IT OFF

steps.t: Clear and organize the work area, and pull mechanical aids for anything you'd otherwise muscle
steps.w: Muscle a pump or an HVAC component into place instead of reaching for the aid and your back takes the strain the aids are there to keep off it.

steps.t: Assemble to the drawings with calibrated tools, holding alignment and clearances as you go
steps.w: An out-of-cal tool lies to you. Alignment and clearances read right when they aren't, and you've built the equipment failure straight into the unit.

steps.t: Control the pinch points every time you bring two parts together for fit-up
steps.w: Hands where the gap closes. Two parts coming together at fit-up is the pinch injury this SOP tells you to stop work for - and by then it's already happened.

steps.t: Run every fastener to the torque spec and write down the critical values
steps.w: Leave a fastener short of spec and you've built in the failure - that's the fastener security QC is looking for and the equipment failure that stops the job. Nothing written down and nobody can prove the joint was ever right.

steps.t: Inspect the assembly for alignment, fastener security and completeness before it's released
steps.w: Release it short a fastener and the first person to find out is the one standing next to it when it comes apart.

steps.t: Stop the job and get supervision if a component drops, somebody gets pinched, or equipment fails
steps.w: Work through it and the dropped part, the crushed hand or the failing unit gets a second crack at somebody.

title: MOBILE SANDBLASTING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 1/9/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Get the JSA completed and reviewed before anything gets pressured up
steps.w: No JSA and nobody has reviewed what's out there. You find the overhead, the buried utility or the people working near you the hard way - after the nozzle is live.

steps.t: Walk the work area - overhead hazards, underground utilities, who else is working near you, what's environmentally sensitive, anything confined or restricted
steps.w: Skip the walk and the area bites you mid-job: something overhead you never looked up at, a utility under your feet, people closer than you thought, or a confined or restricted space nobody flagged.

steps.t: Set your barricades, hang the signage, and mark the exclusion zone
steps.w: No barricade, no zone, no warning. Nothing stops an unauthorized hand from walking in behind you and into the stream before either of you knows he's there.

steps.t: Inspect the whole rig before you run it - blast pot, hoses, fittings, deadman, compressor, moisture separator - damage, leaks, does it work - and anything defective comes out of service
steps.w: A split hose, a loose fitting or a deadman that won't release is the equipment failure this SOP makes you stop the job for, except you find it with the pot loaded and your hand on the nozzle. Leave it in the pile instead of pulling it and the next hand inherits it.

steps.t: Suit up before you touch the nozzle - blast hood on Grade D supplied air, glasses under the hood, hearing protection, gloves, blast suit, steel-toes
steps.w: Bare in a blast cloud is the silica exposure this SOP trains you on, straight into your lungs, and abrasive into unprotected eyes. Hood with no supplied air is worse - you're just breathing the dust in a closed box.

steps.t: Don't pull the deadman until the barricades are up and every hand is clear of the exclusion zone
steps.w: Hot nozzle with people still inside the line. That's the injury the whole zone exists to prevent, and the man who takes it never saw the stream coming.

steps.t: Stay in constant communication with your support man the whole time you're blasting
steps.w: Hood down, air roaring, nobody watching you. You go into respiratory distress inside that helmet - one of the emergencies this SOP names - and nobody knows until somebody wanders over.

steps.t: Off the trigger the second you lose visibility, the gear malfunctions, or conditions turn unsafe
steps.w: Blasting blind means you can't see who walked into the zone. Riding out a malfunction under full pressure is the equipment failure this SOP tells you to stop for - hold the deadman through it and it turns into an injury or an uncontrolled release of abrasive.

steps.t: Contain the spent abrasive, blasted coating and debris to the extent practicable - that's part of the job, not cleanup somebody else does
steps.w: Loose spent abrasive and stripped coating blow into whatever's environmentally sensitive around you. That's an uncontrolled release of abrasive, and this SOP makes you stop the job when it happens.

title: PAINT, PREP AND COATING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Get trained on the coating system, SDS review, ventilation, fire prevention and PPE before you touch the job
steps.w: You're handling a product nobody walked you through. The first hazard that comes out of that can is one you have no answer for.

steps.t: Safety glasses, coating gloves and steel-toe boots on - respirator and FR clothing when the job calls for it
steps.w: Coating on bare skin and vapor straight into your lungs. The respirator sitting on the bench was the one thing between you and that exposure.

steps.t: Walk the job first - specs, surface condition, ambient conditions, ventilation, ignition sources and barricading
steps.w: An ignition source nobody looked for, vapor with nowhere to go, and no barricade keeping foot traffic out of the spray.

steps.t: Prep the surface to the specified cleanliness before any coating goes on
steps.w: Coating laid over a dirty surface never bonds. It lets go of the surface later and the job gets done a second time.

steps.t: Mix and apply exactly the way the manufacturer data sheet says - no shortcuts off the sheet
steps.w: Mixed off the data sheet, it never cures. You're standing in the same vapor stripping a coat that should have gone on once.

steps.t: Keep ventilation running and the fire watch posted where it's required
steps.w: Vapor stacks up in a dead-air corner with nobody watching for a spark. That's exactly the fire the watch was standing there to catch.

steps.t: Check film thickness and cure as you go
steps.w: Thin spots and a coat handled before it's cured. It gets ruined, and the job comes straight back to you.

steps.t: Shut the job down for a spill, fire or exposure - notify supervision and start the response
steps.w: A spill spreads or a hand gets dosed and the spray keeps running because nobody called it. Supervision hears about it once it's already big.

steps.t: Contain the overspray and handle the waste to project requirements before you walk away
steps.w: Overspray drifts onto everything downwind and the waste ends up wherever it lands. That's the environmental hit the whole job gets measured on.

title: PRESSURE PIPE WELDING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Don't strike an arc unless you're a qualified welder and your WPQR is current
steps.w: A lapsed ticket and nobody looked. An unqualified bead is the only thing holding high pressure, and it lets go as a leak or a fire with a hand standing right at the joint.

steps.t: Verify drawings, materials, WPS, joint prep, fit-up, preheat and the exclusion zone before you start
steps.w: Wrong material, cold steel, sloppy fit-up, and the joint still looks finished when you're done with it. It fails in service instead - and the exclusion zone you never set is why somebody is standing there when it does.

steps.t: Hood down, FR clothing, gloves and eye protection on, respiratory protection if the job calls for it
steps.w: Nothing between you and the arc. Your eyes take the flash, your own clothes are what burns when a fire starts, and you breathe whatever comes off that metal all shift.

steps.t: Run the weld strictly to the WPS parameters - no drifting off the sheet
steps.w: Off the WPS is off code, and code compliance and integrity are the whole reason this procedure exists. You've put a joint in a high-pressure line that no inspector can accept, and it opens up once there's full pressure behind it.

steps.t: Control heat input, interpass temperature and cleanliness pass to pass
steps.w: Heat runs away, interpass climbs, contamination goes into the joint. That's the weld that leaks first, and it leaks with the system at full pressure.

steps.t: Stop work the moment the job deviates from the approved WPS
steps.w: You watched it drift and kept burning. Every pass after that deviation is weld nobody approved sitting in a high-pressure line, and there's no record telling the next man to go look for it.

steps.t: Stop work and notify supervision the second you get a leak, a fire or an injury
steps.w: You keep the arc going while it's leaking or burning. Supervision never hears about it, nothing gets stopped, and the leak or fire this procedure told you to stop for is left to grow with men still on the joint.

steps.t: Document the welds and sign off the hold points as you go
steps.w: No weld record, no signed hold points. There's nothing showing that joint was ever made to the WPS and nothing for the inspector to accept - so it can't be accepted, and it can't proceed.

steps.t: Get the visual and NDE done as specified - nothing proceeds until it's accepted
steps.w: Pressure goes into a system nobody accepted. The flaw the NDE would have caught is sitting behind full pressure now, and it finds you as a leak.

title: RIGGING AND LIFTING
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Don't touch the rigging unless you're trained and authorized for it
steps.w: An untrained hand makes up the pick and nobody in the bay knows it's wrong. You find out when the load comes off the slings.

steps.t: Hard hat, gloves, safety glasses, steel-toe boots, and hi-vis as required - on before you step in
steps.w: Skip the hard hat and the steel toes and a dropped load finds the parts of you that had nothing over them. Skip the hi-vis and nobody clears you out of the path that load is about to travel.

steps.t: Plan the pick - load weight, center of gravity, rigging configuration, and the travel path
steps.w: Guess the weight and the center of gravity and the load rolls out of the slings on the first pick, over ground nobody walked first.

steps.t: Inspect the rigging before it goes on the load - every time
steps.w: Rigging you never looked at parts under load. Everything it was holding drops, and it drops onto whatever is under it.

steps.t: Any damaged sling or hardware comes out of service right then - tag it and pull it
steps.w: Leave damaged gear in the rack and the next crew grabs it. Same damage, new dropped load, and you handed it to them.

steps.t: Stay inside the rated capacity of every piece of gear in the pick
steps.w: Load it past its rating and the rigging is the thing that fails. That's a dropped load, and everything under it is in the way.

steps.t: Run tag lines on the load - control it from the line, not with your hands
steps.w: No tag line, no control. The load gets away from you and the only thing left to steady it with is your hand.

steps.t: Keep communication clear with everyone on the lift, start to finish
steps.w: Crossed signals and the load moves before the crew is clear. That's the near miss - assuming it stays a near miss.

steps.t: Stop the job for a dropped load, a near miss, or an injury - and call supervision
steps.w: Crew keeps lifting after a drop and whatever caused it is still in the rigging for the next pick. Supervision hears about it when somebody's hurt.

title: SHOP TOOLING, MACHINES AND CNC
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Be trained on this exact machine before you put hands on it
steps.w: Nobody ever walked you through this one and you learn what it does at full speed, with your hands already inside it.

steps.t: Safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves as appropriate, steel-toe boots - on before you start
steps.w: No glasses and the first thing off the tool finds your eye. No plugs and the shop takes your hearing a shift at a time. No boots and the tooling you fumble lands on your foot.

steps.t: Verify every guard is in place and the emergency stops actually work
steps.w: Guard off or a dead e-stop and there's nothing between you and the cutter - and nothing to kill it with when it goes wrong.

steps.t: Check the tooling condition and lock the workpiece down hard
steps.w: Chewed-up tool or a loose part - the workpiece breaks free and leaves the machine faster than you can step back.

phases.name: RUN IT AND LOCK IT OUT

steps.t: Run the machine inside the manufacturer's limits - whatever this machine is rated for
steps.w: Push it past what it was rated for and the tool or the machine lets go mid-cut, at full spindle speed, pointed at you.

steps.t: Leave the guards where they are - no bypassing to get a better look
steps.w: Reach past a guard you pulled and the moving tooling can't tell your hand from the work.

steps.t: Stay aware the whole time it's running - the machine and everybody near it
steps.w: Tune out and you miss the cut going wrong, or the guy who walked into the chip line behind you, until it's already an injury.

steps.t: Machine acts up or somebody gets hurt - stop it and notify supervision
steps.w: Keep feeding a machine that's malfunctioning and the small problem becomes the injury, with nobody upstream told to stop the job.

steps.t: Apply lockout/tagout before any maintenance or servicing
steps.w: No lock, no tag. Someone hits start while your hands are in it and the machine does exactly what it was built to do.

title: STRUCTURAL WELDING
sub: FRAMES, RAILS AND SKIDS - MAGTEC ALASKA, KENAI AK
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Check the welder is qualified with a current WPQR before any structural bead goes down
steps.w: Paper's expired and nobody looked. Now an unqualified hand is laying structural bead, and nothing about that joint is proven. The frame goes out and nobody can honestly say it will hold.

steps.t: Hood, FR clothing, gloves, eye protection - and respiratory protection if the job calls for it
steps.w: Bare skin and no hood. The arc burns your eyes, the sparks find your arms, and the fume goes straight down your throat all shift.

steps.t: Work the pre-job: drawings, materials, joint prep, fit-up, preheat and distortion controls
steps.w: Wrong material, sloppy fit-up, no distortion control. You burn a day of rod into a frame that pulls out of square and no longer matches the drawing - and it gets cut back out.

steps.t: Weld it to the approved WPS - no shortcuts off procedure
steps.w: Off procedure, that joint's strength is whatever you happened to give it, not what the approved procedure called for. Nobody can stand behind it.

steps.t: Hold your heat input and interpass temperature where the procedure puts them
steps.w: Miss the procedure's numbers and you are not welding to the WPS anymore. The steel pulls, the rail comes out of square, and the joint is no longer the one the drawing specified.

steps.t: Keep the joint clean - cleanliness is part of the procedure, not housekeeping
steps.w: Weld into a dirty joint and its integrity is unproven, which is the one thing this procedure exists to protect. It comes back as a repair you have to document, or a piece inspection will not release.

steps.t: Document the welds and any repairs as you go
steps.w: No record, no proof of what went into that joint or what got repaired. Inspection has nothing to check against, and the piece does not get released.

steps.t: Visual inspection and NDE as specified before the piece is released
steps.w: Released unchecked, the defect leaves with the frame. Inspection before release is the last place anybody is looking - past that point the piece is carrying load on trust instead of proof.

title: WPS COMPLIANCE
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Have the current controlled WPS and WPQR at the weld station before you strike an arc
steps.w: That copy taped to the wall is last year's. Every pass you lay comes off an uncontrolled procedure, and it's a non-compliance the day somebody pulls the file.

steps.t: Check your own qualification is current for the WPS you're about to run
steps.w: Ticket's lapsed and none of that is qualified work. Only a current-qualified hand is allowed to weld to that WPS, so every pass you laid is outside the procedure and the file behind the joint can't say otherwise.

steps.t: Verify the WPS matches the job - material, joint configuration and position - before you weld
steps.w: Right WPS, wrong joint or wrong position. The whole run is outside procedure, and it's a stop-work the moment anybody catches it - after you've already filled the bevel.

steps.t: Weld inside the WPS parameters - every pass, no drifting off the sheet
steps.w: Drift off what that sheet calls for and you're not running that WPS any more. You're running something nobody qualified, on a joint going out the door as if they had.

steps.t: Get engineering approval in hand before you change any WPS parameter
steps.w: Change it on your own hook and there's no approval standing behind that weld - just you, filling in for engineering.

steps.t: Stop work and notify supervision the moment the documentation is invalid or conditions go unsafe
steps.w: Burn through it and the bad paper or the unsafe condition is still there for the next hand - only now it's welded shut and nobody upstream ever heard about it.

title: WELDING TABLE SETUP
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Hood, FR's, gloves, eye pro and steel toes on before you touch the table
steps.w: Arc lights and you're a layer short. This SOP names all five - hood, FR's, gloves, eye pro, boots - as required before the work starts. Skip one and the burn lands on the exact piece of you that wasn't covered.

steps.t: Verify the table is level and every fixture is locked down
steps.w: Out of level, fixture loose. That's the instability this SOP tells you to stop work for - the part walks mid-pass and the joint comes back out with a grinder.

steps.t: Check the table ground is adequate before anything gets clamped
steps.w: No solid ground, no return path. The current picks its own way off that table, and the burn or the fire it starts is the emergency this SOP stops work for.

steps.t: Don't start until a supervisor has verified the setup and the materials
steps.w: This SOP puts setup and materials on the supervisor, not on you alone. Skip that check and a bad setup or the wrong stock rides all the way to weld-out before anybody catches it.

steps.t: Clean the joints and verify fit-up
steps.w: Dirty joint, sloppy gap. This SOP exists for accurate fabrication - you just bought the opposite, and it gets cut back out.

steps.t: Confirm the materials and the WPS before you strike an arc
steps.w: Wrong material, wrong procedure. Every inch you run is off-spec and the piece comes apart on the table to do it again.

steps.t: Position components securely, keep the work area clear, and set yourself up to reach the joint without contorting
steps.w: Loose part on a crowded table. It shifts while you're hooded up and blind - that's the instability this SOP stops work for, and you never see it coming.

steps.t: Clear debris and slag out of the work area
steps.w: Cut-offs and slag underfoot. This SOP calls those trip hazards for a reason - you step back hooded, catch a foot, and go down hard next to the table you were just welding on.

title: LADDERS AND ROLLING SCAFFOLD
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Get trained on ladders and scaffold before you set foot on either one
steps.w: Untrained hand on a scaffold finds out what it does wrong while standing on it - and there is nothing under you but the drop.

steps.t: Safety glasses on, proper footwear, fall protection if the job calls for it
steps.w: Wrong boots on a rung and nothing clipped off. Your foot goes and there is nothing between you and the ground.

steps.t: Walk the ladder or scaffold and look it over for defects before you use it
steps.w: A cracked rail or a chewed-up rung does not warn you. It lets go with your full weight on it and you ride it down.

steps.t: Lock the scaffold wheels before anybody steps on the deck
steps.w: Wheels free. You lean into the work, the scaffold rolls out from under you, and you go down with it.

steps.t: Guardrails in place, and stay off the top rungs unless the ladder is built for it
steps.w: No rail and your boots on the top rung - one stumble and there is nothing to grab and nothing to stop the fall.

steps.t: Maintain three points of contact - two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand
steps.w: Down to two points and the rung slips. Nothing is left holding you to the ladder.

steps.t: Do not overreach - however close the work looks, it is not close enough
steps.w: Reach past the rails and your weight goes with you. The ladder walks out sideways and you are off it before you know you are falling.

steps.t: Anything goes unstable or somebody gets hurt - stop the work and tell supervision
steps.w: You ride out the wobble instead of calling it, and the first thing supervision hears about it is the injury.

title: ZOOM BOOM
meta: SOP v1.1 - Rev 1 03/2026 - Approved D. Redick - Condensed from a summary-level SOP; chronology inferred from workflow

steps.t: Make sure the hand in the seat is trained and authorized on the telehandler - nobody else runs it
steps.w: Nobody untrained finds out what this machine does wrong at a convenient moment. They find it out with a load up and a crew standing around them.

steps.t: Hard hat, hi-vis, safety glasses, gloves and steel-toe boots on before you climb in
steps.w: No hi-vis and you're just another shape in the yard to the next machine through. No steel toes and a dropped fork finds your foot.

steps.t: Walk the pre-use inspection - tires, forks and attachments, hydraulics, alarms, brakes, and the load charts
steps.w: Skip it and you find the soft tire, the weeping hydraulic or the dead alarm the hard way: load up, machine moving, nothing stopping it.

steps.t: Read the ground before you set up - bearing capacity and slope. Unstable surface, you don't run
steps.w: Soft ground doesn't hold. One side settles under the tire, the machine leans past the point it comes back from, and it goes over with you in it.

steps.t: Set your exclusion zone and put a spotter on it to keep pedestrians out
steps.w: No zone, no spotter, and somebody cuts under the load on their way to the next bay. Nothing that heavy stops in time.

steps.t: Stay inside rated capacity and work off the load chart
steps.w: Past the chart the back end goes light. The boom keeps reaching, the machine pivots forward over the front tires, and the load comes down on whoever is in front of it.

steps.t: Keep your footing stable, travel with the load low, and put a spotter on any blind side
steps.w: Load carried high rides top-heavy over every rut in the yard. Blind side with nobody watching and the forks find a man before you do.

steps.t: Shut it down and call supervision the second you get a malfunction, a tip-over feel, or an injury
steps.w: Nurse a bad machine along and the next thing to let go, lets go with a load in the air and somebody under it.

steps.t: Park it out: forks down on the deck, parking brake set, keys out before you walk away
steps.w: Forks left up is a raised steel edge in a yard full of people walking. Keys left in is somebody with no business in that seat driving it off.
